name: Chemistry
description: Introductory chemistry covering atomic structure, the periodic table, chemical bonding, reactions, stoichiometry, states of matter, solutions, acids and bases, and basic thermodynamics.

modules.title: Matter & Measurement
modules.objectives: Classify matter by state and properties; apply SI units and significant figures to measurements. Students will use vocabulary, models, and evidence to interpret examples, support scientific explanations, and connect the concept to the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Chemistry 2e §1.3 — physical and chemical properties and changes.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Module 1: Matter & Measurement.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Use this provided evidence table: copper wire—solid, reddish-brown, bends without breaking; distilled water—liquid, colorless, freezes at 0°C; oxygen—gas, colorless, supports a glowing splint in a supervised laboratory; table salt—white crystalline solid, dissolves in water; candle wax—solid, melts near a flame and resolidifies on cooling. Do not repeat any test. Classify each state and one physical property; use the supplied oxygen and wax observations to distinguish a chemical property from a physical change. Convert 2.50 cm to meters, 35.0 mL to liters, and 0.00450 kg to grams, preserving significant figures. Submit: one labeled PDF, document, or worksheet. Include: cited observations, conversions with units, and significant-figure reasoning. Evaluation: safe use of supplied evidence, accurate classification, units, significant figures, and readable organization.

modules.title: Atomic Structure
modules.objectives: Identify subatomic particles; calculate atomic number, mass number, and understand isotopes; describe the Bohr model. Students will use vocabulary, models, and evidence to interpret examples, support scientific explanations, and connect the concept to the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Chemistry 2e §2.3 — protons, neutrons, electrons, isotopes, and atomic symbols.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Module 2: Atomic Structure.
modules.video2Note: Crash Course Chemistry #1 — The Nucleus and Atomic Structure
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Using the periodic table, complete an atom profile for five different elements: list protons, neutrons (for the most common isotope), electrons, atomic number, and mass number. Submit a table with all calculations shown, one Bohr or electron-shell diagram for each element, and a short explanation of how atomic number and mass number reveal subatomic structure. Submit: one labeled PDF, document, or clear scan containing the five atom profiles and shell diagrams. Include: reasoning that supports each conclusion, the isotope named for each element, proton/neutron/electron calculations, atomic and mass numbers, and a short explanation of how the two numbers differ. Evaluation: accurate particle counts, explicit isotope assumptions, legible diagrams, and consistent notation.

modules.title: Electron Configuration
modules.objectives: Write electron configurations using orbitals and quantum numbers; identify valence electrons and predict periodic trends. Students will use vocabulary, models, and evidence to interpret examples, support scientific explanations, and connect the concept to the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Chemistry 2e §6.4 — electron configurations, orbital filling, and valence electrons.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Module 3: Electron Configuration.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Write full and abbreviated electron configurations for Na, Cl, Fe, and O. Circle the valence electrons for each and predict which element has the highest electronegativity based on configuration. Submit: one labeled PDF, document, or clear scan containing all eight configurations and the electronegativity prediction. Include: orbital-filling order, noble-gas cores, valence-electron labels, and a periodic-trend justification. Evaluation: correct configurations, accurate valence counts, valid trend reasoning, and clear notation.

modules.title: The Periodic Table
modules.objectives: Describe the organization of the periodic table into periods and groups; distinguish metals, nonmetals, and metalloids; explain trends in atomic radius, electronegativity, and ionization energy.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Chemistry 2e §6.5 — periodic trends and their atomic explanations.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Module 4: The Periodic Table.
modules.video2Note: Crash Course Chemistry #3 — The Periodic Table
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Create a mini periodic table for elements 1–20. For each element, label it as metal, nonmetal, or metalloid and indicate whether atomic radius increases or decreases across the period and down the group. Submit: one labeled PDF, document, or clear scan of the mini periodic table. Include: classifications for all 20 elements, arrows showing trend directions across periods and down groups, and two sentences explaining effective nuclear charge and occupied shells. Evaluation: accurate placement and classification, correct trend directions, evidence-based explanation, and readable design.

modules.title: Chemical Bonding
modules.objectives: Distinguish ionic and covalent bonds; draw Lewis structures; apply VSEPR theory to predict molecular shape; determine polarity. Students will use vocabulary, models, and evidence to interpret examples, support scientific explanations, and connect the concept to the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Chemistry 2e §7.6 — VSEPR geometry, bond dipoles, and molecular polarity.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Module 5: Chemical Bonding.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Draw Lewis structures for H₂O, NH₃, CO₂, and CH₄. For each, predict the molecular geometry using VSEPR theory and determine whether the molecule is polar or nonpolar. Submit valence-electron counts, bond/lone-pair labels, geometry names, polarity decisions, and a 1–2 sentence justification for each molecule. Submit: one labeled PDF, document, or clear scan containing all four molecular analyses. Include: total valence-electron counts, Lewis structures with lone pairs, electron-domain and molecular geometries, bond-polarity reasoning, and net molecular polarity. Evaluation: correct electron accounting, valid VSEPR shapes, justified polarity, and legible structures.

modules.title: Chemical Nomenclature
modules.objectives: Name and write formulas for ionic compounds, molecular compounds, acids, and polyatomic ions. Students will use vocabulary, models, and evidence to interpret examples, support scientific explanations, and connect the concept to the module assignment.

modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Module 6: Chemical Nomenclature.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Name the following compounds: NaCl, CaCO₃, HNO₃, SO₂, Fe₂O₃, and NH₄Cl. Then write formulas for magnesium chloride, sulfuric acid, nitrogen dioxide, and copper(II) sulfate. Submit a classification for each compound (ionic, covalent, acid, or polyatomic-ion compound), show charge-balancing work where needed, and correct these two intentionally flawed entries: “sodium chlorine” for NaCl and Ca₂O for calcium oxide with explanations. Submit: one labeled PDF, document, or clear scan containing the ten names/formulas and two corrections. Include: reasoning that supports each conclusion, compound classification, oxidation states or prefixes, charge-balancing work for ionic compounds, and the naming rule used for each correction. Evaluation: correct nomenclature and formulas, explicit charge balance, accurate classifications, and clear explanations.

modules.title: Chemical Reactions & Balancing
modules.titleZh: 化学反应与方程式配平
modules.objectives: Given chemical formulas or word equations, balance coefficients so each element has equal atom counts on both sides; classify common synthesis, decomposition, single-replacement, double-replacement, and combustion patterns; justify cases that reasonably fit more than one descriptive category.

modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Module 7: Chemical Reactions & Balancing.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Balance and analyze these equations: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O; CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu; NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O; CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. For each, show an atom count before and after balancing and identify the most useful reaction pattern, noting any case that could reasonably receive more than one label. Submit: one labeled PDF, document, or worksheet containing all five balanced reactions. Include: smallest whole-number coefficients, atom-count tables before and after, pattern labels, any defensible overlap note, and the conservation explanation. Evaluation: unchanged formulas, conserved atoms, correct coefficients, defensible classification, and clear reasoning.

modules.title: Stoichiometry
modules.objectives: Use the mole concept and molar mass to perform stoichiometric calculations; identify limiting reagents and calculate percent yield.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Chemistry 2e §4.3 — mole ratios, limiting reactants, and yield.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Given the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O: (a) Calculate moles of H₂O produced from 4 mol H₂. (b) If 5 g of H₂ reacts with 32 g of O₂, identify the limiting reagent. (c) Using the reactant quantities from part (b), calculate percent yield if 30 g of H₂O is actually collected. Submit: one labeled PDF, document, or clear scan containing parts (a)–(c). Include: reasoning that supports each conclusion, the balanced mole ratios, molar-mass conversions, limiting-reagent comparison, theoretical yield used for part (c), units at every step, and percent-yield calculation. Evaluation: correct stoichiometric chain, identified limiting reagent, internally consistent yield basis, significant figures, and readable work.

modules.title: States of Matter & Gas Laws
modules.objectives: Apply kinetic molecular theory to gas behavior; solve problems using Boyle's, Charles's, Avogadro's, and ideal gas laws. Students will use vocabulary, models, and evidence to interpret examples, support scientific explanations, and connect the concept to the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Chemistry 2e §9.2 — gas variables and the ideal gas law.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Module 9: States of Matter & Gas Laws.
modules.video2Note: Crash Course Chemistry #16 — Ideal Gas Laws
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: For a fixed amount of ideal gas, solve three supplied cases: use Boyle’s law for 3.0 L at 100 kPa compressed to 1.5 L; use Charles’s law for 2.0 L warmed from 300 K to 600 K at constant pressure; and use PV = nRT for 22.414 L at 273.15 K and 1.000 atm with R = 0.082057 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹. State the held-constant variables and explain why Kelvin is required. Submit: one labeled PDF, document, or worksheet containing all three gas-law cases. Include: the selected law, held-constant variables, Kelvin temperatures, substitutions with units, results with sensible significant figures, and an ideal-gas assumptions note. Evaluation: correct law selection, algebra, units, temperature scale, assumptions, and interpretation.

modules.title: Solutions
modules.objectives: Describe factors affecting solubility; calculate solution concentration using molarity; perform dilution calculations; explain colligative properties. Students will use vocabulary, models, and evidence to interpret examples, support scientific explanations, and connect the concept to the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Chemistry 2e §3.3 — molarity, solution preparation, and concentration calculations.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Calculate the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 58.5 g of NaCl in enough water to make 1.0 L of solution. Then determine the volume of 2.0 M HCl needed to prepare 500 mL of 0.5 M HCl using the dilution formula. Submit: one labeled PDF, document, or clear scan containing both concentration problems. Treat 1.0 L as the final solution volume for the NaCl calculation. Include: reasoning that supports each conclusion, mole conversion, M=n/V, M₁V₁=M₂V₂, units, and a sentence distinguishing solution volume from solvent volume. Evaluation: correct formulas, conversions, volume interpretation, significant figures, and clear work.

modules.title: Acids, Bases & pH
modules.objectives: Apply Arrhenius and Brønsted-Lowry definitions; calculate pH and pOH; describe neutralization reactions and titration. Students will use vocabulary, models, and evidence to interpret examples, support scientific explanations, and connect the concept to the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Chemistry 2e §14.2 — pH, pOH, and hydrogen and hydroxide ion concentrations.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Module 11: Acids, Bases & pH.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Calculate the pH of: (a) a solution with [H⁺] = 0.001 M, (b) a 0.1 M NaOH solution. Then write the balanced neutralization equation for HCl reacting with NaOH and calculate how many mL of 0.5 M NaOH is needed to neutralize 20 mL of 0.5 M HCl. Submit: one labeled PDF, document, or clear scan containing both pH calculations, the balanced neutralization equation, and the titration calculation. Include: [OH⁻] or pOH reasoning for NaOH at 25°C, mole ratios, M×V units, and final volumes. Evaluation: correct acid–base model, pH/pOH work, balanced equation, stoichiometry, units, and assumptions.

modules.title: Thermochemistry
modules.objectives: Distinguish endothermic from exothermic processes; calculate enthalpy changes using calorimetry and Hess's Law. Students will use vocabulary, models, and evidence to interpret examples, support scientific explanations, and connect the concept to the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Chemistry 2e §5.2 — heat transfer and calorimetry calculations.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Calculate q for 50.0 g of water heated from 20.0°C to 80.0°C using c = 4.18 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹, and classify the water’s energy change. Then use these supplied equations: C(s)+O₂(g)→CO₂(g), ΔH = −393.5 kJ; 2CO(g)+O₂(g)→2CO₂(g), ΔH = −566.0 kJ. Reverse or scale equations as needed to determine ΔH for C(s)+½O₂(g)→CO(g). Submit: one labeled PDF, document, or worksheet containing the calorimetry and Hess’s-law analyses. Include: q=mcΔT with units, the system sign convention, every equation reversal or scaling, cancellations, and the summed target equation. Evaluation: correct calculation, signs, equation manipulation, cancellation, units, and reasoning.

modules.title: Reaction Rates & Equilibrium
modules.objectives: Identify factors that affect reaction rates; apply Le Chatelier's principle; interpret equilibrium constants. Students will use vocabulary, models, and evidence to interpret examples, support scientific explanations, and connect the concept to the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Section 13.3, for Le Chatelier predictions and equilibrium shifts; use the GIIS module video for the linked reaction-rate review.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Module 13: Reaction Rates & Equilibrium.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: For the equilibrium N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) (exothermic, at constant temperature except in part b): predict the shift when (a) pressure increases because the container volume decreases at constant temperature, (b) temperature increases, (c) H₂ is added, and (d) NH₃ is removed. Write the equilibrium expression Kc for this reaction. Submit: one labeled PDF, document, or clear scan containing all four predictions and Kc. Include: the stress applied, predicted shift, the equilibrium feature that counters the stress, phase-appropriate Kc terms, and an explanation that a catalyst changes rate but not K. Evaluation: correct Le Chatelier reasoning, accurate expression, explicit assumptions, and clear cause-and-effect explanations.

(c) Identify the functional group in ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) and name the class of organic compound. Submit: one labeled PDF, document, or clear scan containing all three parts. questions.question: Which of the following is a physical change?
questions.explanation: Melting changes only the physical state of H₂O; its chemical identity remains water.

questions.question: The atomic number of an element equals:
options: The number of electrons plus neutrons
questions.explanation: The atomic number is defined by the number of protons in the nucleus and therefore identifies the element.

questions.question: Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons but differ in their number of:
questions.explanation: Isotopes remain the same element because proton count is unchanged, but their neutron counts and mass numbers differ.

questions.question: How many valence electrons does a neutral sulfur atom in Group 16 have?
questions.explanation: Sulfur is a main-group element in Group 16, whose neutral atoms have six valence electrons.

questions.question: Which trend is correct for atomic radius moving left to right across a period?
questions.explanation: Across a period, effective nuclear charge generally increases while shielding changes little, pulling electrons closer and decreasing radius.

questions.question: In the simple ionic model of sodium chloride, bonding begins when:
options: Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine, forming oppositely charged ions
Both atoms share two electron pairs equally
Two neutral atoms remain unchanged but touch
Chlorine transfers a proton to sodium
questions.answer: Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine, forming oppositely charged ions
questions.explanation: In the simple NaCl model, electron transfer forms Na⁺ and Cl⁻; their electrostatic attraction constitutes the ionic bond.

questions.question: What is the molecular geometry of H₂O?
questions.explanation: Oxygen has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs; four electron domains give tetrahedral electron geometry and a bent molecular shape.

questions.question: Which option best completes this statement: The correct name for the compound NaCl is...
questions.explanation: Na forms Na⁺ and Cl forms Cl⁻; ionic nomenclature names the metal first and changes chlorine to chloride.

questions.question: In the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, the coefficient in front of H₂O is:
questions.explanation: Balancing gives 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O, so the water coefficient is 2. This coefficient gives four H atoms and two O atoms on each side of the equation.

questions.question: One mole of any substance contains approximately:
questions.explanation: One mole contains the Avogadro constant, approximately 6.022×10²³ specified entities.

questions.question: The molar mass of H₂O is approximately:
questions.explanation: Using about 1.008 g/mol for H and 16.00 g/mol for O gives 2(1.008)+16.00≈18.02 g/mol.

questions.question: Which temperature unit should be used in gas law calculations such as PV = nRT?
questions.explanation: PV=nRT requires absolute temperature; Kelvin begins at absolute zero and preserves proportional gas-law relationships.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a physical property and a chemical property. Give one example of each for iron.
questions.answer: A complete response should answer this prompt directly: A physical property (e.g., density, melting point) can be observed without changing composition; a chemical property (e.g., rusting/oxidation) describes how a substance reacts and changes identity.
questions.explanation: A physical property can be measured without changing iron’s identity, such as density; a chemical property describes its ability to form new substances, such as rusting.

questions.question: Draw the Lewis structure for CO₂ and predict its molecular shape. Is the molecule polar or nonpolar? Explain.
questions.answer: A complete response should answer this prompt directly: CO₂ has two double bonds between C and each O, linear geometry (VSEPR), and is nonpolar because the bond dipoles cancel due to symmetry.
questions.explanation: CO₂ has two C=O double bonds and a linear geometry. The equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, making the molecule nonpolar.

questions.question: Balance the following equation and identify its reaction type: CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. Then explain what conservation of mass means in the context of this reaction.
questions.answer: A complete response should answer this prompt directly: Balanced: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Combustion reaction. Conservation of mass means the number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides; matter is neither created nor destroyed.
questions.explanation: CH₄+2O₂→CO₂+2H₂O is a combustion reaction. Each side has one C atom, four H atoms, and four O atoms, demonstrating conservation of mass.

questions.question: At constant temperature, what happens to a gas sample's volume if its pressure doubles?
questions.explanation: Boyle's Law shows pressure and volume are inversely proportional at constant temperature.

questions.question: Which expression defines molarity?
options: Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
Moles of solute per liter of solution
Grams of solute per liter of solvent
Moles of solvent per liter of solution
questions.answer: Moles of solute per liter of solution
questions.explanation: Molarity M=n/V is moles of solute divided by liters of total solution. The denominator is solution volume, so definitions based on solvent mass describe molality instead.

questions.question: At 25°C, a solution with pH=3 is best described as:
questions.explanation: At 25°C, pH values below 7 are acidic; pH 3 corresponds to [H⁺]=1×10⁻³ M. This describes the solution’s acidity and does not by itself identify whether the dissolved acid is chemically strong or weak.

questions.question: According to Brønsted-Lowry theory, an acid is a:
questions.explanation: A Brønsted–Lowry acid donates H⁺, while a Brønsted–Lowry base accepts H⁺. The definition applies to proton transfer and is broader than producing hydroxide ions in water.

questions.question: What happens to heat energy during an endothermic reaction?
options: Heat is absorbed from the surroundings
Heat is released to the surroundings
Heat is converted entirely into mass
questions.answer: Heat is absorbed from the surroundings
questions.explanation: Endothermic reactions absorb heat from their surroundings. The reacting system gains energy while the surroundings lose it, which corresponds to a positive ΔH for the system.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes Hess's law?
options: Enthalpy depends only on the path taken
The total enthalpy change is independent of the reaction pathway
Only exothermic reactions obey conservation of energy
questions.answer: The total enthalpy change is independent of the reaction pathway
questions.explanation: Because enthalpy is a state function, the net ΔH depends only on initial and final states. Reaction steps may be reversed, scaled, and added to obtain the target equation.

questions.question: Increasing the concentration of reactants generally:
options: Has no effect on reaction rate
questions.explanation: Higher reactant concentration usually produces more frequent effective collisions, increasing reaction rate when other factors are fixed.

questions.question: Le Chatelier's principle predicts that adding more product to an equilibrium system will shift the reaction:
questions.explanation: Adding product is a stress; the system shifts toward reactants to consume part of the added product.

questions.question: What particles make up an alpha (α) particle?
questions.explanation: An alpha particle is the same as a helium nucleus: two protons and two neutrons.

questions.question: Which process describes nuclear fission?
options: Combining small nuclei to form a larger nucleus
Splitting a heavy nucleus into smaller fragments
The emission of an electron from the nucleus
questions.answer: Splitting a heavy nucleus into smaller fragments
questions.explanation: Fission splits a heavy nucleus into smaller nuclei and typically releases neutrons and energy.

questions.question: After two half-lives, how much of an original radioactive sample remains?
questions.explanation: Each half-life multiplies the remaining amount by 1/2, so two half-lives leave (1/2)²=1/4.

questions.question: The functional group –OH (hydroxyl) is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Alcohols contain a hydroxyl group bonded to a saturated carbon; other listed groups have different carbon–oxygen arrangements.

questions.question: Colligative properties depend primarily on which feature of a solution?
options: The identity of the solvent only
The number of solute particles present
questions.answer: The number of solute particles present
questions.explanation: Colligative properties depend on how many solute particles are dissolved, not mainly on their identity.

questions.question: In a calorimetry experiment, q = mcΔT. If m = 100 g, c = 4.18 J/g°C, and ΔT = 5°C, what is q?
questions.explanation: q=mcΔT=(100 g)(4.18 J/g°C)(5°C)=2090 J. The units cancel to joules: grams and degrees Celsius cancel the matching factors in the specific heat.

questions.question: Which gas law combines Boyle's, Charles's, and Avogadro's laws into a single equation?
questions.explanation: PV=nRT relates pressure, volume, amount, and absolute temperature in one ideal-gas equation.

questions.question: The limiting reagent in a chemical reaction is:
options: The reagent present in the largest amount
The reagent that is completely consumed first and limits product formation
The reactant with the highest molar mass
questions.answer: The reagent that is completely consumed first and limits product formation
questions.explanation: The limiting reagent is consumed first according to the balanced mole ratio, so it fixes the maximum amount of product; any other reactant remains in excess.

questions.question: Explain dynamic equilibrium using H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI. What is happening at the molecular level when equilibrium is reached?
questions.answer: A complete response should answer this prompt directly: At dynamic equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates, so concentrations show no net change. In H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, HI forms and decomposes at the same rate while molecular collisions and reactions continue.
questions.explanation: A complete response states that the forward and reverse rates are equal, concentrations have no net change, and reactions continue at the molecular level.

questions.question: A student dissolves 117 g of NaCl (molar mass = 58.5 g/mol) in enough water to make 2.0 L of solution. Calculate the molarity of the solution and describe how you would further dilute it to 0.5 M.
questions.answer: A complete response should answer this prompt directly: Moles of NaCl = 117 / 58.5 = 2.0 mol. Molarity = 2.0 mol / 2.0 L = 1.0 M. To dilute to 0.5 M: use M₁V₁ = M₂V₂; take 500 mL of the 1.0 M solution and add water to make 1.0 L total.
questions.explanation: First, 117 g ÷ 58.5 g/mol=2.0 mol and 2.0 mol ÷ 2.0 L=1.0 M. Then M₁V₁=M₂V₂ shows that 500 mL of stock diluted to 1.0 L gives 0.5 M.

questions.question: Compare alpha, beta, and gamma radiation in charge, approximate mass, and penetrating ability. Explain why internal alpha exposure can be especially hazardous without claiming that one radiation type is always most dangerous.
questions.answer: A complete response should answer this prompt directly: Alpha particles have +2 charge, mass about 4 u, and low external penetration but dense ionization over a short range. Beta particles have −1 charge and very small mass with moderate penetration. Gamma rays have no charge or rest mass and high penetration. If an alpha-emitting material is inhaled or ingested, nearby tissue can receive concentrated ionization; actual risk still depends on isotope, activity, dose, location, and exposure time.
questions.explanation: A complete answer distinguishes penetration from ionizing effect and makes the hazard claim conditional on dose and exposure route.

questions.question: Electronegativity generally increases:
options: Down a group and left to right across a period
Down a group and right to left across a period
Up a group and left to right across a period
Up a group and right to left across a period
questions.answer: Up a group and left to right across a period
questions.explanation: Electronegativity generally rises left to right with effective nuclear charge and rises up a group as atomic radius decreases.

quizQuestions.question: Which state of matter has a definite volume but no definite shape?
quizQuestions.explanation: Liquids retain nearly fixed volume but flow to adopt the shape of their container.

quizQuestions.question: The SI base unit for mass is:
quizQuestions.explanation: The kilogram, not the gram or pound, is the SI base unit for mass. A gram is one-thousandth of that base unit, while pounds are outside the SI system.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is a chemical property?
quizQuestions.explanation: Flammability describes whether a substance can combust and form new substances. Density, color, and melting point can be observed without changing composition.

quizQuestions.question: A balance reads 12.40 g. Which digit is the estimated digit reported by the instrument?
quizQuestions.explanation: In an analog or rounded measurement, the final reported digit is the estimated digit; here that is the 0 in the hundredths place.

quizQuestions.question: How many significant figures are in 4.050 g?
quizQuestions.explanation: The interior zero and the trailing zero after the decimal point are significant, so all four digits count.

quizQuestions.question: The particle in an atom with no electrical charge is the:
quizQuestions.explanation: A neutron has no net electric charge; protons are positive and electrons are negative.

quizQuestions.question: The mass number of an atom equals:
quizQuestions.explanation: Mass number counts nucleons, so it equals protons plus neutrons. Electrons are not included because their masses are negligible and mass number is defined from the nucleus.

quizQuestions.question: Carbon-12 and Carbon-14 are:
quizQuestions.explanation: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have six protons but different neutron counts, making them isotopes.

quizQuestions.question: In the Bohr model, electrons orbit the nucleus in:
quizQuestions.explanation: The Bohr model places electrons in quantized shells, although the modern quantum model uses orbitals rather than fixed paths.

quizQuestions.question: An isotope has atomic number 8 and mass number 18. How many neutrons does it have?
quizQuestions.explanation: Neutrons equal mass number minus atomic number: 18−8=10. Atomic number 8 fixes the proton count at 8, leaving 10 of the 18 nucleons as neutrons.

quizQuestions.question: The Aufbau principle states that electrons fill orbitals:
options: Starting from the highest energy level
Starting from the lowest available energy level
Two at a time in separate orbitals first
quizQuestions.answer: Starting from the lowest available energy level
quizQuestions.explanation: The Aufbau principle fills the lowest available energy orbitals first. Hund’s rule separately governs the distribution among equal-energy orbitals.

quizQuestions.question: How many electrons can a 2p subshell hold?
quizQuestions.explanation: A p subshell contains three orbitals, and each orbital can hold two electrons with opposite spins, giving a maximum of 3×2=6 electrons.

quizQuestions.question: The electron configuration of oxygen (atomic number 8) is:
quizQuestions.explanation: Eight electrons fill as 1s²2s²2p⁴ after lower-energy orbitals are occupied first.

quizQuestions.question: Which statement is required by Hund’s rule?
options: Electrons occupy equal-energy orbitals singly before pairing
Electrons fill the highest-energy orbital first
An orbital may contain three electrons
Paired electrons in one orbital have the same spin
quizQuestions.answer: Electrons occupy equal-energy orbitals singly before pairing
quizQuestions.explanation: Hund’s rule places one electron in each equal-energy orbital before any pair forms.

quizQuestions.question: How many valence electrons are shown by 1s²2s²2p⁵?
quizQuestions.explanation: The highest principal level is n=2, containing 2s² and 2p⁵ for 2+5=7 valence electrons.

quizQuestions.question: Elements in the same group of the periodic table have the same number of:
quizQuestions.explanation: Main-group elements in one group usually share a valence-electron count, which helps explain similar chemistry.

quizQuestions.question: Metalloids (semimetals) are found:
options: Far left of the periodic table
Far right of the periodic table
Along the staircase boundary between metals and nonmetals
In the middle transition metals only
quizQuestions.answer: Along the staircase boundary between metals and nonmetals
quizQuestions.explanation: Metalloids lie along the zigzag staircase separating most metals from nonmetals, reflecting their mixture of metallic and nonmetallic properties.

quizQuestions.question: First ionization energy generally increases:
options: Left to right across a period
Right to left across a period
Moving to the center of a period
quizQuestions.answer: Left to right across a period
quizQuestions.explanation: Across a period, increasing effective nuclear charge generally makes it harder to remove an electron, so first ionization energy rises.

quizQuestions.question: The halogen group elements are found in group:
quizQuestions.explanation: Halogens occupy Group 17 and commonly have seven valence electrons. Periodic position and effective nuclear charge explain the trend, so a nearby element provides a useful reasonableness check.

quizQuestions.question: Which atom is expected to have the larger atomic radius, Na or Cl?
options: Na, because radius generally decreases across Period 3
Cl, because radius generally increases across Period 3
They are equal because they share a period
Cl, because it has fewer occupied shells
quizQuestions.answer: Na, because radius generally decreases across Period 3
quizQuestions.explanation: Across a period, increasing effective nuclear charge generally pulls valence electrons closer, so Na is larger than Cl.

quizQuestions.question: Which statement best defines ionic bonding?
options: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
Equal sharing of electrons between all atoms
Transfer of protons between two neutral atoms
quizQuestions.answer: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
quizQuestions.explanation: An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions; common introductory examples form after electron transfer.

quizQuestions.question: What information does a Lewis structure show?
options: The three-dimensional shape of a molecule
Valence electrons as dots around the atomic symbol
quizQuestions.answer: Valence electrons as dots around the atomic symbol
quizQuestions.explanation: Lewis structures display valence electrons as bonds and lone pairs. They do not by themselves show the complete three-dimensional molecular geometry.

quizQuestions.question: VSEPR theory predicts molecular shape based on:
options: Atomic mass of the central atom
Repulsion between electron pairs around the central atom
quizQuestions.answer: Repulsion between electron pairs around the central atom
quizQuestions.explanation: VSEPR predicts shape by arranging bonding and lone electron pairs around a central atom to minimize their electrostatic repulsions.

quizQuestions.question: Which molecule is nonpolar even though it contains polar bonds?
quizQuestions.explanation: CO₂ is linear, so its two equal C=O bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.

quizQuestions.question: A central atom has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs. What is its molecular shape?
quizQuestions.explanation: Four bonding domains arrange tetrahedrally to minimize electron-pair repulsion. With no lone pairs on the central atom, the molecular shape matches the electron-domain geometry.

quizQuestions.question: The compound Fe₂O₃ is named:
quizQuestions.explanation: Each oxide ion is −2, so three oxide ions total −6; two iron ions must total +6, making each Fe(III).

quizQuestions.question: The formula for calcium nitrate is:
quizQuestions.explanation: Ca²⁺ requires two nitrate ions, NO₃⁻, to make a neutral formula unit: Ca(NO₃)₂.

quizQuestions.question: The prefix 'tetra-' in covalent nomenclature indicates:
quizQuestions.explanation: The molecular prefix tetra- denotes four atoms of the named element. Thus carbon tetrachloride contains four chlorine atoms, while tri- and penta- would indicate three and five.

quizQuestions.question: Acids that contain oxygen are called:
quizQuestions.explanation: An oxyacid contains hydrogen, oxygen, and another element; its name derives from the oxyanion.

quizQuestions.question: The name of HCl when dissolved in water is:
quizQuestions.explanation: HCl(g) is hydrogen chloride, but HCl(aq) is named hydrochloric acid. The aqueous state triggers binary-acid naming: hydro- plus the chloride root and the suffix -ic acid.

quizQuestions.question: A synthesis reaction has the general form:
quizQuestions.explanation: A synthesis pattern combines two or more reactants into one product: A+B→AB.

quizQuestions.question: In complete combustion, a hydrocarbon reacts with O₂ to produce:
quizQuestions.explanation: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon converts its carbon to CO₂ and its hydrogen to H₂O; coefficients are then chosen to conserve each element.

quizQuestions.question: When balancing a chemical equation, you may only change:
quizQuestions.explanation: Coefficients change particle ratios without changing substance identities; changing a subscript would create a different substance.

quizQuestions.question: Which coefficients balance CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O?
quizQuestions.explanation: One carbon gives one CO₂; four hydrogens give two H₂O; the products then contain four oxygen atoms, requiring two O₂.

quizQuestions.question: One mole of carbon-12 has a mass of:
quizQuestions.explanation: By definition, one mole of carbon-12 atoms has a mass of 12 g; the isotope provides the historical basis for the mole and atomic-mass scale.

quizQuestions.question: How many moles are in 36 g of H₂O (molar mass = 18 g/mol)?
quizQuestions.explanation: Use n=m/M: 36 g ÷ 18 g/mol=2 mol. The gram units cancel, leaving the amount in moles.

quizQuestions.question: Mole ratios in stoichiometry come from:
options: Atomic masses on the periodic table
Coefficients in the balanced chemical equation
The number of electrons in each atom
quizQuestions.answer: Coefficients in the balanced chemical equation
quizQuestions.explanation: Balanced-equation coefficients give the relative amounts in moles of reactants consumed and products formed, so they supply stoichiometric mole ratios.

quizQuestions.question: The limiting reagent is the reactant that:
options: Is present in the greatest moles
Is completely used up first and determines maximum product
Requires the most energy to react
quizQuestions.answer: Is completely used up first and determines maximum product
quizQuestions.explanation: The limiting reagent is used up first at the balanced reaction ratio. Once it is gone, no more product can form even if another reactant remains.

quizQuestions.question: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 20.0 g and an actual yield of 15.0 g. What is the percent yield?
quizQuestions.explanation: Percent yield=(actual/theoretical)×100=(15.0/20.0)×100=75.0%. The balanced coefficients give mole ratios; dimensional analysis then connects amount, mass, limiting reagent, and yield.

quizQuestions.question: According to kinetic molecular theory, gas particles:
options: Have strong attractive forces between them
Occupy most of the container volume
quizQuestions.explanation: In the ideal-gas model, particles move continuously and randomly between elastic collisions.

quizQuestions.question: Boyle's Law states that at constant temperature, pressure and volume are:
quizQuestions.explanation: At constant temperature and amount, PV is constant, so increasing pressure decreases volume.

quizQuestions.question: Charles's Law states that at constant pressure, volume and temperature are:
options: Inversely related by a squared factor
quizQuestions.explanation: At constant pressure and amount, V/T is constant when temperature is measured in Kelvin.

quizQuestions.question: A gas occupies 2.0 L at 300 K. At constant pressure, what volume would it occupy at 450 K?
quizQuestions.explanation: Charles’s law gives V₂=V₁(T₂/T₁)=2.0(450/300)=3.0 L. Gas-law comparisons require a fixed amount of gas, stated held-constant variables, and absolute temperature in kelvin.

quizQuestions.question: Which change doubles the pressure of a fixed amount of ideal gas at constant volume?
quizQuestions.explanation: At fixed n and V, P is directly proportional to absolute temperature, so doubling Kelvin temperature doubles pressure.

quizQuestions.question: Solubility of most solid solutes in water increases with:
quizQuestions.explanation: For many solid solutes in water, higher temperature increases solubility, though this is an empirical trend with exceptions.

quizQuestions.question: A solution is 2.0 M NaCl. This means:
options: 2.0 mol NaCl per liter of solution
2.0 mol NaCl per kg of solvent
2.0 g NaCl per kg of solvent
quizQuestions.answer: 2.0 mol NaCl per liter of solution
quizQuestions.explanation: A 2.0 M solution contains 2.0 moles of solute per liter of total solution. The volume is the final solution volume, not merely the amount of solvent used to prepare it.

quizQuestions.question: Which equation relates concentration and volume before and after a dilution?
quizQuestions.explanation: M₁V₁=M₂V₂ expresses conservation of solute during dilution: adding solvent changes concentration and total volume but not the moles of solute transferred.

quizQuestions.question: Boiling point elevation is an example of a:
quizQuestions.explanation: Boiling-point elevation is colligative because its ideal magnitude depends mainly on the concentration of dissolved particles rather than their chemical identity.

quizQuestions.question: Which change is a colligative effect of adding a nonvolatile solute to water?
options: The solvent becomes a new element
The solute’s identity alone sets the effect
quizQuestions.explanation: Dissolved particles lower the solvent’s freezing point; the size of the ideal colligative effect depends mainly on particle concentration.

quizQuestions.question: According to the Arrhenius definition, a base is a substance that produces ______ ions in water.
quizQuestions.explanation: An Arrhenius base increases hydroxide-ion concentration when dissolved in water.

quizQuestions.question: At 25°C, how is an aqueous solution with pH 7 classified?
quizQuestions.explanation: At 25°C, a neutral aqueous solution has equal [H⁺] and [OH⁻] and pH 7. The 25°C condition matters because the neutral pH value changes slightly with temperature.

quizQuestions.question: In a neutralization reaction, an acid reacts with a base to form:
quizQuestions.explanation: A typical acid–base neutralization forms water from H⁺ and OH⁻ plus an ionic salt.

quizQuestions.question: In NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, which species is the conjugate acid of NH₃?
quizQuestions.explanation: NH₃ accepts H⁺ to become NH₄⁺, so NH₄⁺ is its conjugate acid. Conjugate acid–base partners differ by one proton, and NH₄⁺ has one more proton than NH₃.

quizQuestions.question: If [H⁺]=1×10⁻⁴ M at 25°C, enter the pH.
quizQuestions.explanation: Use pH=−log₁₀[H⁺]. Because [H⁺]=1×10⁻⁴ M, the negative base-10 logarithm is 4.

quizQuestions.question: Which statement correctly describes enthalpy?
options: H=U+PV; at constant pressure with only PV work, ΔH equals heat transferred
H is identical to reaction speed
H is the number of moles present
H is always equal to temperature
quizQuestions.answer: H=U+PV; at constant pressure with only PV work, ΔH equals heat transferred
quizQuestions.explanation: Enthalpy is the state function H=U+PV. For a constant-pressure process with only pressure-volume work, ΔH=qₚ.

quizQuestions.question: An exothermic reaction has a ΔH value that is:
quizQuestions.explanation: An exothermic system releases heat, so its enthalpy change is negative. Using the system perspective, heat leaving the system makes products lower in enthalpy than reactants.

quizQuestions.question: What quantity does calorimetry measure?
options: Heat exchanged during a chemical or physical process
quizQuestions.answer: Heat exchanged during a chemical or physical process
quizQuestions.explanation: Calorimetry determines heat exchanged by measuring a temperature change in a system with known mass and heat capacity, often using q=mcΔT.

quizQuestions.question: The specific heat of water is 4.18 J/g°C. This means:
options: It takes 4.18 kJ to heat 1 g of water by 1°C
It takes 4.18 J to raise 1 g of water by 1°C
quizQuestions.answer: It takes 4.18 J to raise 1 g of water by 1°C
quizQuestions.explanation: A specific heat of 4.18 J/(g·°C) means 4.18 joules raise one gram of water by one degree Celsius under the stated conditions.

quizQuestions.question: Hess's Law allows us to calculate ΔH by:
options: Adding ΔH values of individual steps in a reaction pathway
quizQuestions.answer: Adding ΔH values of individual steps in a reaction pathway
quizQuestions.explanation: Hess’s law adds the ΔH values of reaction steps after reversing or scaling them as needed, because enthalpy depends only on the initial and final states.

quizQuestions.question: Increasing temperature generally increases the reaction rate because:
options: It gives more particles enough energy to overcome the activation energy barrier
It changes the equilibrium constant only
quizQuestions.answer: It gives more particles enough energy to overcome the activation energy barrier
quizQuestions.explanation: Higher temperature raises average kinetic energy and increases the fraction of collisions with enough energy to overcome the activation barrier.

quizQuestions.question: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by:
options: Providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy
quizQuestions.answer: Providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy
quizQuestions.explanation: A catalyst supplies an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, increasing successful collisions without being consumed or changing equilibrium.

quizQuestions.question: Le Chatelier's principle states that if a stress is applied to a system at equilibrium, the system will:
options: Reach a new equilibrium favoring the stress direction
Shift to relieve the stress and reach a new equilibrium
Increase the rate of both forward and reverse reactions equally forever
quizQuestions.answer: Shift to relieve the stress and reach a new equilibrium
quizQuestions.explanation: After a change in concentration, pressure, or temperature, an equilibrium system shifts in the direction that partially counteracts the imposed change.

quizQuestions.question: What does a catalyst change for a reversible reaction already at equilibrium?
options: It speeds both directions and does not change the equilibrium composition
It shifts equilibrium permanently toward products
quizQuestions.answer: It speeds both directions and does not change the equilibrium composition
quizQuestions.explanation: A catalyst lowers activation barriers for both directions. Equilibrium is reached faster, but K and the equilibrium composition do not change.

quizQuestions.question: If Kc is much greater than 1, which side generally predominates at equilibrium?
quizQuestions.explanation: Kc≫1 means the product terms dominate the equilibrium ratio, so products generally predominate.

quizQuestions.question: What nuclear change occurs during beta-minus (β⁻) decay?
options: A nucleus emits an alpha particle
A neutron converts to a proton and emits an electron
A nucleus absorbs a gamma ray
quizQuestions.answer: A neutron converts to a proton and emits an electron
quizQuestions.explanation: In beta-minus decay, a neutron changes into a proton while an electron and an antineutrino are emitted, increasing atomic number by one.

quizQuestions.question: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is:
options: The time for half the atoms to gain a proton
The time for half of the radioactive atoms to decay
The half of its atomic mass
The time for its radiation to decrease by 100%
quizQuestions.answer: The time for half of the radioactive atoms to decay
quizQuestions.explanation: Half-life is the time required for the number of undecayed radioactive nuclei in a sample to fall to half its initial value.

quizQuestions.question: Nuclear fusion releases energy by:
options: Combining light nuclei (such as hydrogen) into a heavier nucleus
Emitting gamma rays from a heavy atom
quizQuestions.answer: Combining light nuclei (such as hydrogen) into a heavier nucleus
quizQuestions.explanation: Fusion combines light nuclei into a heavier nucleus; the decrease in total mass is released as energy according to mass–energy equivalence.

quizQuestions.question: The simplest organic compound class, containing only C–C and C–H single bonds, is:
quizQuestions.explanation: Alkanes are hydrocarbons containing only carbon–carbon and carbon–hydrogen single bonds.

quizQuestions.question: Which observation best supports classifying CH₃CH₂OH (ethanol) as an alcohol?
options: It contains a hydroxyl (–OH) group bonded to carbon
It contains a carbon–carbon double bond
It contains only carbon and hydrogen
quizQuestions.answer: It contains a hydroxyl (–OH) group bonded to carbon
quizQuestions.explanation: Ethanol contains a hydroxyl group attached to a carbon framework, the defining functional group of an alcohol.
